text: Hey folks; I’m the author of RemainderBot. Given your goals and task lists, it writes PRs that complete those tasks for you using excess Claude & Codex subscription tokens. As the founder of Bakeoff, I spend my time on customer development and engineering architecture & review. RemainderBot solves two problems for me and I suspect for many others out there: * There are many small tasks that require a few minutes of my time and need my context, but I just don’t have the mental energy to prioritize them, do a context shift, perform a small amount of work, and finalize the results a dozen times a day. * Some weeks I don’t get close to my Claude and Codex subscription limits. It has accomplished quite a bit - 111 PRs including customer call prep, a census of 31 GitHub orgs’ agent setup files, and standalone prototypes to demo to engineers I meet with. You interact with it in whatever interface you use with GitHub PRs. It uses your comments and decisions on whether to merge PRs to guide which kinds of tasks and approaches it takes in the future. RemainderBot runs either as a manual process on your machine or as a cronjob on a server. In tick (cronjob) mode, it checks how much subscription quota is left and how much time there is until the weekly reset before picking a task and creating a PR. Here’s how you get started: * Check that git, claude (or codex), and gh CLIs exist and are authenticated on your machine * Clone the openremainderbot repo: git clone https://github.com/arimwilson/openremainderbot.git remainderbot cd remainderbot cp -n GOALS.example.md GOALS.md cp -n sources.example.toml sources.toml Edit those two files with your personal goals and with sources for your task lists, respectively. Finally: python3 -m remainderbot snapshot python3 -m remainderbot run --provider claude --deadline-minutes 20 --size small These commands will pick a task, work on it in a new branch, and will cost you a few percent of your weekly quota. Please drop a comment on what it did for you and if it got anything wrong here or in https://github.com/arimwilson/openremainderbot/discussions/6 :). This is a common failure mode for AI: frequently it does what you tell it to, but then its attention mechanism isn't on things like security or robustness and so it unknowingly introduces a crash or memory safety violation. text: I was a game developer for many years, at large scale (MMO) and at small scale (indie). With the advent of AI, I've been _trying_ to use AI to accelerate game development and have come to a few conclusions. 1. AI models want to make everything deterministic. This sounds like a truly sound way to write a verifiable program. Games are not verifiable simulators except in the niche of ...simulators. Even in those cases, the vast infrastructure devoted to this leads to a lot of churn, bugs (AI forcing things to align with the verifier), and rigidity. 2. Making a game != Fun. This one is obvious but needs to be stated. Anyone on earth right now can say "make me doom" or "make me a super mario clone" and Opus/Astra will dutifully comply and make something generic and bland. Once the novelty of "oh wow it actually built it" wears off, you're left with a mediocre clone, lacking depth, that no customer would want hoisted upon them. 3. Content and novelty are the hard parts. AI models always create the mediocre middle. There's real work (and interesting work) involved in both inventing novel gameplay systems which LLMs will never stumble upon despite infinite 'brainstorming prompts'. But, AI is 'OK' at taking your novel idea and proposing directions -- that you can then strike down viciously until something interesting emerges. On the content side, this has always been a truism for an independent developer. AI art tools aren't quite there yet. There's image-to-3D and there's Mixamo for animation but we're not there yet. Nearly though! But again, will every game look like a bland generic AI generated image with bland AI generated models? 4. AI models are crap at building re-usable large-scale architectures. Even building with Opus 5.5 and Astra they will happy design themselves into a corner. Yes, they can _also_ design themselves out of that corner at speed - with a lot of pain and code churn and mess. I've found it vastly better to iterate slowly, using your experience (if you have it) to structure the core architecture and systems the way you want (AI writing the code) -- and then build upon that solid base -- taking special care to reject updates that butcher your architecture. I think this applies to most coding projects actually. 5. Game dev currently surfaces very clear differences in model capabilities with Opus 5.5 leading the pack (in this domain) and Fable 5.1 and Astra/GPT-6.1 Sol following a decent distance behind. Part of this is wrong usage of the tool. If you say "make a game" -- Opus will outperform the others by a large margin -- in making a generic "game" that was undefined (a paragraph of text is not a defined game). In these cases, the model has filled in all the gaps in undefined areas with average 'what probably looks good' content. You're left with something devoid of creativity. This is the problem with the myriad three.js tech demos. If you instead have a clear understanding of what you're building, models (nearly all SOTA) will get you there cheaper by building what you've asked without speculation. I don't believe you should hand off the one human worthwhile trait, creativity, to the AI -- so "Opus build a game" is indeed the wrong way. 6. It seems hard (and pointless) to collaborate with other human developers when AI coding on smaller/indie projects. Each AI model is trying to "solve the whole thing". The speed also makes it hard to stop at arbitrary boundaries and promotes a rushed feeling or conversely a sluggish feeling (AI did all the stuff, now I'm waiting to integrate with a friend/collaborator). This is probably easily solvable but has thus far felt weird when I've collaborated. 7. The return of custom engines? While models do great with Godot and Unreal, this is the chance to build custom engines like the golden years of the 2000s. OK, this one is a bit of nostalgia but I miss the world of dozen of game engines each with their own unique look and feel. Otherwise you get XBOX 360 era where every "realistic" character looks like a Gears of War meathead. Every adventure game has the same mechanics, you're hooking something, you're scooting under something, you're scooting between walls or things, you're on collapsing things that require either button sequences or hitting your 'hook' (every adventuring has some hook of infinite rope of course). OK, this entire bullet is just a rant about samey-ness. LLMs should unlock our human creativity and allow experimentation outside of that cost imposed same-ness. All things said, it's _clear_ that the acceleration is here if you know what you want. You can go from concept to prototype in a few hours. You then have to be disciplined enough to step back and rebuild that thing (with AI) correctly and towards a useful objective that you've thought up. I'm looking forward to went content creation catches up. Or perhaps that's a sad day when creativity vanishes.

text: I think that they're essentially solving the wrong problem. Imagine that you have git but you don't even have a concept of programming language more complex than assembly. All your commits and git history are pure assembly. Everything is cool, until one day C++20 randomly spawns into existence, and a bunch of guys decide to use it in the company. The issue is, the compiler generates so much assembly, that your existing workflow cannot keep up with it. Your assembly git repo grows into hundreds of gigabytes, with PRs that are pretty much complete rewrites coming every single day and there's no way to review any of that shit. What Anthropic is doing is redoing git from scratch so that it can handle all that assembly, while the correct thing to do is to commit C++ code into the repo, with deep trust that you'll never hit a bug in the compiler - basically impossible for initial versions of compilers, taken for granted nowadays. What I'm saying is, Anthropic should create a versioning system for prompts, because they are the true "source code". Given the same prompt and the same sequence of random numbers, LLM will generate exactly the same code, which sounds awfully close to how compilers work. Once in a while put the generated code as a point of reference+ caching and presto.

In particular: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_in_compilation > In the copyright law in the United States, such copyright may exist when the materials in the compilation (or "collective work") are selected, coordinated, or arranged creatively such that a new work is produced. Copyright does not exist when content is compiled without creativity, such as in the production of a telephone directory. In the case of compilation copyright, the compiler does not receive copyright in the underlying material, but only in the selection, coordination, or arrangement of that material. All my experience seeing orgs ship real production code with the assistance of AI over months/many-thousands-of-commits shows that the skill not only lies in what context you choose to provide in the first place (product and technical specifications, design guidelines, prompting process with the model(s)), but also in how to effectively review and test all of it, which is still done with human direction throughout. This is why people with no experience in coding can't do with AI what an industry veteran with 20 years shipping to production can. In any case, I think existing reading of copyright law will be sufficient to say that large AI-driven software projects are a process of orchestration and also of curation in selecting what actually gets committed (or, if commit-by-default is enabled, then what to revert). This may not always be true in the future, though, as capabilities increase...one part of me thinks you could just do random stuff like "Make me an excel except every cell is a powerpoint presentation" and a good enough AI would reason through and produce something without further input. But I think in most cases, folks have a real set of requirements in mind, and get all of them into the AI through a process of iteration in various ways. I think that's real work that requires skill and, in many cases, creativity, at least in the sense that someone else walking up to the same tool and prompting on their own would produce a very different output than you'd see if you asked the same person to retry the same project. Time will tell.

text: We still do code review but it does bottleneck how much we can ship. I'm looking at what we can do to alleviate this. Here's what I think the near future may look like, as far as getting more value per time spent out of human code review. I'm coming at this from the POV of an org that still mandates human code review and I think a lot of this advice doesn't hold if you are all-in on the black box software factory approach. If you're reviewing code you're responsible for, your job now is to provide stewardship of its long term technical direction even if you are not personally reading and writing every line of code. This means preserving the coherence of designs past and present, and ensuring that they are not being worked around in service of a short-term goal. Stop reading every line of every file to look for minor gotchas. Focus on core business logic and whether invariants are modeled well & to the fullest extent possible by the type system. Agents are better than most humans now at spotting insane gotchas. At least one frontier model should review most PRs. In the before times, you could argue that TODO comments and small nits on PRs should be addressed, because most likely they'd never get attention again once the PR merges. Now, small issues should instead be automatically recorded and followed up on quickly by another agent. Minor code quality issues should become rules, and old code should be constantly revisited by agents to bring it up to par with new code. Provide the transcripts of the session with the PR. Look for evidence of thoughtful direction & solid premise behind the conversation that led to the PR being made. In addition to providing more mentorship opportunities to the author, this also discourages meat proxying/low-value-added uses of AI. Asking someone to rewrite or completely discard a PR that's just a bad idea should no longer be the ego bruising event it once was (at least with respect to the cost sunk to make the PR). Require a higher bar for proving that code works and stays working. The testing pyramid IMO should now be more of a testing hourglass. Or an upside-down pyramid, even. Automated E2E tests should be abundant. Every feature should receive adequate manual testing by an agent, with proof of work. In the vein of "stays working," look for good observability and guardrails around a feature. If you're doing a good job of leveraging agents to keep code up to par, this means adding (and cycling out) feature flags, ensuring that there's adequate logging, having a cohesive monitoring solution with good coverage, and a plan for what to do if there's an issue in prod.

I prefer the term "Ultimate Things", to de-emphasize how useless they are. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Useless_machine >The Italian artist Bruno Munari began building "useless machines" (macchine inutili) in the 1930s. He was a "third generation" Futurist and did not share the first generation's boundless enthusiasm for technology but sought to counter the threats of a world under machine rule by building machines that were artistic and unproductive.[ >The version of the useless machine that became famous in information theory (basically a box with a simple switch which, when turned "on", causes a hand or lever to appear from inside the box that switches the machine "off" before disappearing inside the box again) appears to have been invented by MIT professor and artificial intelligence pioneer Marvin Minsky, while he was a graduate student at Bell Labs in 1952. Minsky dubbed his invention the "ultimate machine", but this nomenclature did not catch on. The device has also been called the "Leave Me Alone Box". So here's a live demo of an ultimate thing I pleasure programmed: https://hyperties.org/cabinet/ultimate/ What this is: I've been using Claude to recreationally developing a PDP-7 and Type 340 vector graphics display emulator, in order to run an early CAD system called PIXIE, which has the first known radial menus, driven by a light pen, developed at Cambridge in the late 1960's, whose 128 pages of PDP-7 assembly language source code the author Heinz Lemke scanned and sent me. Once I got it working, I told Mitch Bradley about how much I wanted a Forth system for it. Mitch has written useful things like OpenFirmware and CForth, and I was his summer intern at Sun in 1987, where we had a great time hacking his CForth into CADroid (a circuit editing system developed at LucasFilms) as an extension language. https://github.com/MitchBradley/openfirmware https://github.com/MitchBradley/cforth http://www.art.net/~hopkins/Don/lang/forth.html Since then, Mitch developed his Sun Forth system into OpenFirmware for the boot ROMs of many like the Sparcstation, PowerPC Mac, and the OLPC. So I thought it would be fun to run Forth on the same machine that ran PIXIE, mainly because I'd love to work together and hack Forth with Mitch again after all these years, but also because Forth was the perfect language for the PDP-7. So Mitch whipped up a PDP-7 Forth in one day with Claude, with Turtle Graphics! https://github.com/MitchBradley/pdp7forth https://hyperties.org/cabinet/forth/ It turns out that the PDP-7 instruction set is ideal for Forth. It has an "XCT" instruction for indirectly executing other instructions, which makes the Forth inner interpreter loop only require 3 instructions. https://github.com/SimHacker/WillWrightShowForFood/blob/main... https://github.com/SimHacker/WillWrightShowForFood/blob/main... Now I'm hacking virtual hardware devices for the PDP-7 and controlling them with Forth. First I made an "Ultimate Machine" device for the PDP-7, inspired by Claud Shannon and Marvin Minsky, whose only purpose is to turn itself off! https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Useless_machine Bruno Munari called it a "Useless Machine", but Minsky was more compassionate, and appreciated its purpose of turning itself off as being ultimately useful, so he renamed it the Ultimate Machine. I think there are some deep implications to the halting problem, but I can't quite put my finger on it the way the Ultimate Machine puts its finger on its own off switch. The Ultimate Machine emulator plugs into the PDP-7 as a virtual device cabinet that has its own device control IOTs that augment the PDP-7 instruction set. DEC sold a lot of "plug-in instruction sets in a cabinet" like the Type 340 vector graphics display, its light pen, character generator, subroutine executer, advanced math instructions, etc. https://gunkies.org/wiki/Type_340_Precision_Incremental_Disp... The Ultimate Machine device, an emulator of device 56 with its registers, phases and IOTs: https://github.com/SimHacker/WillWrightShowForFood/blob/main... https://github.com/SimHacker/WillWrightShowForFood/blob/main... Then I made a Forth program that draws an animation of the Ultimate Machine on the 340 display. It's not a "simulation" -- it's an actual visual representation of the emulated Ultimate Machine device state that FORTH controls via IOT instructions! The Forth 340 view, with the IOT words, the hand, lid and lamps, and the light-pen switch, so you can turn it on (and off) with the light pen: https://github.com/SimHacker/WillWrightShowForFood/blob/main... Then for even more fun, I made a Turing Machine device, which is like the 340 display in that it not only adds device control IOT instructions, but also executes its own Turing Machine code out of the same 18 bit core memory as the PDP-7 and 340 display. https://hyperties.org/cabinet/turing/ https://github.com/SimHacker/WillWrightShowForFood/blob/main... But that was more because through Rails I learned the MVC pattern, learned the layer-middelware pattern from Rack (and the ActiveRecord ORM -- but I now no longer like ORMs but that's a different story). Those 2 pattern I still use today in some way or form, and I find them in many modern (Rust) web development frameworks/libs. So I now no longer use Rails for new projects. These projects were all SSR web apps (traditional server-side rendered web apps that use JavaScript sparingly), built with Kotlin+http4k. Http4k is a web library, so no framework there and it feels very good. The article is very frontend/JS-focussed. I prefer to keep things simpler and just use SSR for the UI. This is because above all (1) I dont like JavaScript (not even when my LLM writes it for me) and (2) for the type of application it is not needed to do state management again in the browser (IMHO it's just more code for the same features). Sure, a little JS is needed in my apps too. But I (assisted by LLM) use it sparingly and when I use it it's with Alpine.js. CSS with Tailwind and JS with Alpine makes for pages that are mostly "self contained" (the CSS and JS defined in the same place as the HTML that relates to it), which makes reasoning about them so much easier. For HTML building i use kotlinx.html (an HTML eDSL in Kotlin; HTML as Kotlin code). I'd say http4k, Tailwind and Alpine are not frameworks. Maybe Alpine is most framework-like of all of these. At least they are not frameworks in the sense that they do not dictate my project folder structure and "how everything ties together". With http4k the "how everything ties together" answer is in your own project's code, NOT in "the framework" or in 3rd party library code. In my latest projects (all LLM assisted) I make heavy use of architecture tests: tests on the shape (e.g.: folder structure) of my codebase. These tests check that my architecture rules are adhered to. Think of enforcing the MVC pattern; only the pattern that I use is way more split out (instead of M-V-C, it more like: boot - contract - db - domain - filter - handler - job - lib - path - presentation - routing - workflow). I'd say framework matter more when: 1. you are learning something, or 2. when the team needs to have shared code hygiene values, or 3. when you do not use architecture tests yet!

Obviously you want memory safety, but there's more than one to get that, and I don't know that you want to force contortions to build simple data structures. text: I was born in 1981, and spent my childhood playing classic games like Dizzy, Ant Attack and Manic Miner on the Sinclair ZX Spectrum. Those games - and so many others - made me want to create my own games. I read every programming book I could find, trying to understand how the developers of the day crammed so much gameplay into such limited machines, with proportionally tiny amounts of CPU power and memory compared to the average systems of today. That fascination led me to a career as a professional software engineer, but I didn’t ship my first real game until very recently. I created Code Like It’s 198x to be the resource I wish I’d had back in the day. Right now, you can start on the ZX Spectrum ( https://code198x.com/systems/sinclair-zx-spectrum/ ), building a series of BASIC games ( https://code198x.com/systems/sinclair-zx-spectrum/basic/ ), or jump straight to Z80 assembly language ( https://code198x.com/systems/sinclair-zx-spectrum/assembly/ ), building your first full game, Meteor Storm ( https://code198x.com/systems/sinclair-zx-spectrum/assembly/m... ). You can work directly in the browser, using the editors, assemblers and emulators I’ve embedded into the site, or you can download the tooling to use separately on Windows, macOS or Linux (Emulators: https://emu198x.github.io , Assemblers: https://asm198x.github.io ). The goals of the site are simple: - Learn about the vintage systems and the cultural context around them - Understand how they worked, what their limitations were, and how developers of the day worked around them - Choose a system, and build a series of games for it in BASIC and/or Assembly (and maybe other languages later) - Build a library of techniques that can be applied not only to games on these systems, but on projects for modern systems too I’m actively working on content for the ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 ( https://code198x.com/systems/commodore-64/ ), NES ( https://code198x.com/systems/nintendo-entertainment-system/ ), and Amiga ( https://code198x.com/systems/commodore-amiga/ ), with other systems to follow based on demand from readers. You can also browse through the Pattern Library ( https://code198x.com/patterns/ ), where I’m attempting to build a set of sample code that you can use in your own games, or explore The Vault ( https://code198x.com/vault/ ), where I’m trying to connect the dots between all of the individuals and companies whose shoulders we stand on today. The longer-term goal is to have a comprehensive set of documentation for each platform, helping readers to understand not only the systems, but the developers who worked with them and the techniques they discovered along the way. Much of this information is already available online, but not in one place, and some of it is buried in forum threads or hard-to-navigate wikis. Focusing on vintage platforms allows us to understand how games are built, without all of the (necessary) abstraction layers that now sit between us and the machine, but many of the techniques are still applicable today - understanding how to write efficient code has never gone out of fashion, even when you have so much more headroom to play with. At this stage, I’m interested in all feedback, positive or negative. If you have experience working on these systems already, I’d very much value your input. If not, please try to follow the lessons through - point out anything I’ve gotten wrong, anywhere the explanations are confusing or where you feel I’ve moved too fast or too slow. If you enjoy the site, or wish it had more content in certain areas, please also let me know - it’ll help guide me. All contributions are also welcome; the site, as well as the supporting tooling, is open-source and freely available, forever. It’s all up on GitHub ( https://github.com/code198x/website ). Caveat: I’ve used AI extensively to help me research and write content for the site; I’ve been careful to reference primary sources wherever possible, and I aim to verify all code samples on the site - not only through my own tooling, but through selected third-party tools as well. Full details of that process are listed on the website.

text: Yes, I have no doubt that AI is going to seriously impact the economy over time. I have lots of doubt that it can impact the economy sufficiently quickly and with enough impact to pay out all the very, very, very large bets being made on it. Even as the AI quality curve has been running ahead of most predictions, its actual impact on the economy has been running well behind. I am watching the dawning realization among the management class that even if coding costs drop to zero, Amdahl's Law means that perhaps productivity doubles for most software engineers, rather than goes to the MOON. AI can help some of the other bottlenecks, but not 100%. On the positive side, we programmers have been trying to collectively explain to management for decades now that our jobs are not just 100% banging away at code on keyboards, we're not just interchangable code monkeys. Well, they're getting their noses rubbed in it now, complete with metrics and charts and all the other things they value more than the feedback from their employees. In fact I was just noticing this week... in the past few months I had been really banging away at a lot of code projects. I was doing that whole "3 or 4 streams going on at once" that many of us have talked about, with a variety of mixed feelings. But in the past few weeks that seems to have starved out. I seem to have burned through the things that I was blocked on code for, and had a reasonable business case to pursue. Now my projects are all blocking up on non-code things again... communication with other teams. Review of documents that are irreducibly things humans need to review. Coordination and planning. I'm still sometimes unblocking multiple things at once and can briefly have multiple projects going, but then I hit a blocker somewhere and I end up unable to continue having multiple simultaneous code projects going at once. Point of all this being that the casual presumption that AI will just utterly destroy the entire economy because it is good at coding may prove to be, well, yeah, exactly the same as the assumption that we are going to all be rich by 2002 because we'll just shift the entire economy to be on the internet and everything will multiply by 1000 in just a couple years as a result. But everything can't be shifted on to the internet. I can't eat a web page. AI can't do everything, and as it advances the things it can't do become a larger and larger percent of the remaining pie as a result. It seems to rhyme a lot with the dot com crash.
label: negative

text: I have had pretty decent success instructing OpenAI/Anthropic models to do this. By default, they don't care too much about human readability (which is understandable) but they're amenable to instruction. - Basic style/linter rules (so you don't get 200-line functions, etc) paired w/ instructing your agent how to use them goes a long way (e.g., a sane rubocop.yml in your repo, plus a note in AGENTS.md telling the agents how to run rubocop, or whatever makes sense for your language) - I have a code review skill that specifically calls out human-readability concerns such as making sure that identifier names represent their contents and intended use The other key IME is that you need to make readability/refactoring passes outside of a particular pull request. When working on a specific branch the LLMs will be somewhat myopic, and do stuff that looks pretty good in isolation, but when you zoom out and look at the bigger picture it's kind of a mess - for example, often they'll duplicate some code that existed elsewhere. The LLMs are also pretty good at generating Mermaid charts and tracing execution flows, which is a great way to understand code. text: We actually experienced this first-hand when building qURL and launching with our initial users as well, it was quite interesting. We knew that what we're building is high impact for AI/agentic world due to the nature of expiring gated-access links for sharing local resources, which is not really something that our competitors (ngrok or cloudflare or tailscale) could offer as well as we could. People were pretty excited, but when we were getting them to try out qurl and running locally, they'd run into all sorts of issue where their coding agent would get confused or distracted and wouldn't actually do the setup we needed them to do (just a few `qurl <param>` commands). It was weird because our docs were public, and github was fully searchable, so we kept wondering why the agent wouldn't just search for it and figure it out? What we realized was that our target audience here, which were largely not-super-technical people who more so cared about vibe coding demos rather than doing proper software engineering (as that wasn't their job), didn't really prompt in the same way as software people like us did. They didn't really "know" how to talk to AI. In particular: they prompted with one-shots and incomplete/unspecific requests, asking for things like `share my app with qurl`; the agent would intuitively know "I have to search for qurl and figure out how to use it", so it would do that; but then, it would ask random other things (to confirm) about homebrew, local setup, preferences, etc. - and since these questions were often roughly technical, many of our users would get derailed and more confused. So, they'd start a conversation with the agent instead of asking it directly, leading to both of them being confused... which would eventually lead to the agent just suggesting something like ngrok or cloudflare to unblock the user's line of questioning. It was weird - but we tested this internally and reviewed the traces, and found that it just came down to prompting habits ultimately: AI is trying to both give you as much info as it can, be as succinct as possible, and also not assume too much about your request all at the same time. It's a REALLLY hard balance to strike. (so it makes sense that it's not perfect) So as a result, when non-technical people were asking to deploy a qurl, the moment the agent would get stuck and need their help, they naturally wouldn't know how to answer or what it was even asking, so the simple request would spiral into its own conversation fork and the `deploy with qurl` point would get lost in context. The prompting advice we came up with for them was this: "if your agent gets stuck, just tell it to search online and figure out how to unblock itself." Because of the balance it tries to strike, it sometimes just needs that little approval to just go and look things up on the internet, even if it is wasting tokens doing so. So the point here isn't so much that it takes skill, but rather it just takes intuition about what AI is good at/bad at and what sort of personality it's being trained to embody. Once you get the hang of that, even if you know nothing about coding at all, you can become pretty effective with your AI toolset simply by virtue of knowing what directions to guide it to and watch pitfalls out for/how to unblock it when needed. Our 2c on the topic!

text: The tension is that most users want something differently generic when they provide a short or vague prompt for creative work. They want to treat the AI like an ideal creative consultant, who not only knows the ideas that are played out and tired but also the ones that they themselves have delivered a dozen times already. They don't want to specify deeper constraints or survey all the cliches and tropes, but they also don't want to generate something that they -- or the people they share the output with -- will immediately recognize as cliche themselves. But LLM's are structured to do exactly the opposite. They discover specific commonalities and tropes and most-frequently-sufficient wells or ley lines that they gravitate towards from whatever their starting point it. You can nudge them away from the most generically cliche tropes by being more detailed in your prompt, but they'll still just find the nearest most right cliche from there. It's what they do and the same quality that makes them tiring and predictable for creative output makes them very useful for things like business communication or coding where landing on such cliches is ideal. To get more variety out, it can be useful to use Perchance-like text-randomization techniques to shuffle combinatoric variations on a prompt before sending it to the model. But that technique is best made available through some kind of special purpose harness for the creative task, not basic chat or direct curl calls to the API.

text: This is one of the biggest benefits. I'm not a plugin user so I don't remember how they're different from skills. Not speaking about the tool in OP specifically but regarding skills in general: you can have essentially the entire task or some of its subtasks (which you'd ordinarily direct to the agent using the skill, the main benefits of which are clearer natural language directions) handled with assistive tools written in any language your environment supports. You can additionally supply the skill with its own config files, data files, etc., building essentially a small repo within particular skills and making these resources however closely tied to the skill as you prefer. This is particularly useful when the agent would otherwise be doing a task that is programmable, or the agent is inconsistent or unable to do it in an efficient, performant or other preferred manner. The programmatic tool assistance means at least some parts of the task (possibly its entirety) could be handled in a well-tested and deterministic manner. How reliable the determinism, optimality, etc. are depends on how well you or the agent writes and verifies the code, tests, spec, etc. in the first place of course, but that only needs to be done correctly once. The other great benefit is reduced token use, potentially a massive reduction. Imagine a task Claude takes 10 minutes to prepare to do because it's reading and analyzing files for the 3rd time in the last 4 minutes, then it's asking for permissions several times in between to do this and that even after you put it in auto mode, then it's "thinking" again for the thousandth time about how to approach the task even though you had it repeat the task a hundred times already...by the time it actually starts doing the task, the most recent models are likely to have churned through tens of thousands of tokens (and that's a conservative estimate for frontier models) in the first 10 minutes. But, with tool assistance, you can have Claude directly handle some parts of that same task which, for example, needs unpredictable analysis or decision-making each time, but also have it use a set of highly optimized programs to handle the bottleneck parts or the parts you want done "your way." You could potentially cut down those 10 minutes of prep time + whatever minutes to actually do the task down to seconds, with barely a couple of thousand tokens used up. Just an example of course, but I've benefited from this strategy repeatedly across various tasks, simple ones and very complex ones. Another great thing is that the tools don't have to be tied to the skill at all, they can live anywhere in your codebase. You could even manually run the scripts to handle certain tasks in their entirety or do the prep work before setting an agent loose on the remainder. There are many different approaches with different advantages. It's like actually using the agent as your...well, agent! But now you're supplying him with the latest gadgets like M/Q does for 007.

text: Your take works in a vacuum, but it lacks the nuance of understand what a model is and what constitutes a parameter in that greater context. >The model is the neural network itself No, and especially not with these LLMs. If someone handed you the "raw" neural network of a modern LLM, you couldn't just run forward passes through it and expect it to behave the same way a proper agent behaves. This should be obvious, but that's an important distinction. Everything else you need to make that neural network behave like an agent are apart of the overall model that we're talking about here. And any parameter of that "everything else" are effectively parameters of the agent itself. Think about a model as a function: you give it some input and it produces some output. A simple model could be something literally like a linear function, f(x) = mx + b. Here, you could say f has two parameters: m and b. That all makes sense and "scales" up to neural networks where there's a lot more parameters, but it's basically just a bunch of these functions where the weights are like m and b in the linear function. But that's not really the full picture for an LLM, right? For example, if you talk about an agent, there inputs you give it would be your prompt and the outputs it produces is whatever text it generates. But what about its system prompt? If that effectively remains fixed, then that's not really an input of the 'function' that is an agent, right? But it does influence the output of the agent. So, from a certain perspective, the system prompt is actually a parameter of the agent. Tweaking that parameter can cause it to produce different outputs for the same input. More importantly, tweaking that parameter can cause it to produce better outputs than it would otherwise. So if you have one agent test another agent by tuning its system prompt such that the output of the second agent is better than it was before, you just had one agent optimize the parameters of another agent. And that's just the system prompt. Think about the overall harness (where the actual codebase can be considered a parameter) or how multiple agents interact with each other and the parameters involved with those kinds of processes. I'm willing to bet you don't buy that explanation, but I can assure you that in machine learning there is a lot of consideration for the parameters which come outside the actual weights of the model, and tuning those parameters can be just as important as tuning the weights of a neural network. I'll say that understanding and accepting this was one of the most important realizations I had while studying ML.

text: This is quite confusing, indeed, but the limits are generous and transparent once you understand the concept. There are two plans, OpenCode Go and Go Plus, for 10$/mo and 40$/mo. With your plan, you get a specific monthly amount of money you can use, with separate weekly and 5-hour limits to not spend all at once. The amount of money you can use depends on the model, but the usage percentage adds up regardless. For example, on the Haiku Model, the monthly limit is 15$/mo, as you read from the page. For other models, such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, the limit is now 80$/mo (the increased it from 60$ recently). This might seem odd, but the stated purpose of OpenCode Go is "Low cost coding models for everyone", so the limits on the open models tend to be higher. The math works like this: You use 5$ no Haiku and 20$ on a 60$ model, then your monthly limit is used 66.6%, meaning 5$ of Haiku or 20$ of a 60$ model remaining. Another way to view this is as follows: You have 10$ flat usage per month, and the "higher usage on each model" is actually just a discount on the token price. So Haiku is discounted to 10$/15$=66.6%, DeepSeek to 12.5% and so on. Go Plus just means you get more usage, though the rate is not always 4x. To answer your remaining questions: The billing is based on the actual provider's api costs, so input/cached/output tokens. I suppose the "requests" number is estimated. The OpenCode TUI and your account website actually show the real session prices, which also helps with an understanding how expensive the agents are on raw (unsubsidized) api pricing. The usage limits are rolling, so there is a 5-hour, a weekly and a monthly limit. The 5h is 20% of the monthly limit, and the weekly is 50% (not sure on the exact numbers). I would agree that the pricing is confusing, but for the price you get surprisingly much usage, especially on the 60$ models. Give DeepSeek V4.1 a try, you get nearly unlimited usage and it's around Sonnet/Opus level.

text: The more constraining the language, the better. For example, languages with strong static typing are better for agents because they reject entire classes of errors. This is why Rust is a particularly good target for coding agents. Its hard to write data races, draw null pointer exceptions, access freed memory, double free memory, etc. Not only that, but the feedback loop becomes shorter because the error happens in the compiler and not when that code path gets run (which may never happen because its so hard to write comprehensive tests). This helps correct the stochastic nature of agents and bring them back on track when they wander. This is the antithesis of the idea that more powerful languages are better but it makes sense. For humans, it costs a lot for the language to get in the way all the time. Yes, a constraining language prevents you from writing errors but it also interrupts flow, forces you to describe processes that are meaningless at the application level, and usually is more verbose. But for an agent, the marginal cost of an additional line of code is less. Both the literal cost but also the opportunity cost. Its not that Rust is a good or bad language per se, its just that agents don't care about ergonomics while humans do. And when you don't have to care about ergonomics this lets you push the tradeoffs way outside the range that would be even remotely acceptable for us. The flip side is that so far, we are in the mix so you can't go all the way to constraints... not that I can imagine what that would look like.
label: neutral

text: Right, let me try and articulate my unease with this decision better. It's not really technical. I'm sure the Anthropic devs did a fantastic job. But... there's a lot of decisions that make sense for a company like Google or Meta that don't make sense for other companies. Google, Meta, Apple and a few others like them are nearly unique. They have extremely profitable quasi-monopolies that have proven impregnable to competitors, and the second price auction system they use automatically sets prices to whatever the market will bear. Thanks to that they they can pay enormous salaries, fund many high risk/low ROI projects and still have lots left over. In such an organization projects like creating your own build system, VCS, IDEs, email system and so on can be rational, even though they can't actually measure the productivity impact of a developer tool to one percentage point of precision. All this is nothing like normal business. Normal businesses face peer competitors, meaning pricing is under continuous downwards pressure. Across all industries the profit margin is only 10%, but that's an average that includes the tech sector. Industries with a lot of competition stabilize at margins around 3% e.g. supermarkets or airlines. When we look at AI labs, what do we see? They spend like they are Google, but the market they're in looks nothing like ads or SaaS. Instead they are in vicious competition selling largely undifferentiated products to price sensitive customers who display almost no brand loyalty. Quite surprisingly to those of us who got used to the FAANG and SaaS era, AI firms look more like airlines than tech firms. In normal companies the rules and culture are totally different. Decisions are driven by people with MBAs who use terms like "core competency", "outsourcing" and "margin compression". In-sourcing is rare because it's expensive and risky. If your margin is only 3% then you don't compete with your own supply chain unless it's absolutely required. Doing that without a shit ton of spreadsheets showing it's necessary is the sort of decision that will get you fired, pronto. You use things off the shelf. If nothing is available for free then you're expected to spend months in vendor negotiations trying to squeeze another 5% off the contract, and this is the kind of work valued in such a culture which is why MBAs rise to the top. Historically the software industry has avoided this because of ads, the ZIRP era, lock-in, the explosive growth of VC up to 2017, and low growth in other sectors like pharma. But that era could never last forever and seems to be ending now. A strong signal is the growth of Bending Spoons, whose business model can be summed up as buying SaaS companies run by people who can't psychologically handle a high interest rate environment and then just running them like a normal business. I realize acutely that the reason I don't run a top tier AI lab is because of this mindset, but if I were running Anthropic I'd be trying to find ways to cut costs dramatically. For a decade+ you never heard the words "tech startup" and "bankruptcy" together in a sentence, partly because VC firms forced firms to acquihire startups that weren't working out, making failure look like success. But this week Character.AI went into Chapter 11. None of us know the true figures but it looks like AI firms don't have the margins to justify acting like a Google or a successful SaaS. Corporate cultures imported from those companies risk blowing everything up.

Problems like context drift, hallucinations, etc that are the result of how attention matrixes and K/V/Q based lookups work as a concept. The way CED is quantized during inference _and_ training it removes positional threshold problems in the final attention matrix lookup. I really recommend reading deepseek's papers, they're really good papers. Having said that, I don't think that letting LLM models write tests or having an "LLM judge" rate the code of another model let alone rate the quality of PRs will help in this regard. It makes context drift problems worse, and it makes the statistical aspects of the positional encoding and thresholds worse. In my opinion, humans should write the tests and design the architecture and its symbol/signature-based contracts between packages/folders. LLMs should fill in the blanks based on the descriptions of branches, and not allowed to modify the human-designed parts. text: When Jev launched last month I assumed it was a novelty. Then we tried it on the job our AI receptionist finds hardest. A caller asks something oddly specific, like whether a free valuation ties them into selling with the agent, and the answer is buried somewhere on the business’s website. We gave Jev a one-line description of every page on the site and asked it one choice question, which page answers this, with “none of these” as the last option. Across four of our customers’ sites (22 to 232 pages) and 168 caller questions, it put the right page first 88% of the time, against 70% for our production embeddings. The number I care about more is how often the LLM got handed the wrong page, 3% against 33%. When the site didn’t have the answer, Jev said so 95% of the time and our current search 23%. Each lookup took about a third of a second, and all 1,449 requests cost about 45 cents. Fair warning, this piece is written for vibe coders and tech business owners rather than engineers, so it’s the plain English version. text: Hi HN. I built Squishling to build LLM “squishability” into services and make it expressible to beautiful Ruby code. The idea: a Ruby class declares what it wants back (a purpose and a strict output schema). Then the LLM can either be the whole logic of the class, or an alternative path / failover when the deterministic pathway fails: class ShipmentUpdate include Squishling purpose "Normalize this carrier's tracking webhook." output_schema do string :status, enum: %w[in_transit out_for_delivery delivered] string :tracking_number end end ShipmentUpdate.call(carrier: "acme-freight", payload: body).squished? # => true It gives engineers the ability to play with system architecture and development pathways allowing, for example, to set up a working integration now and write the code only when you can see the shape of the data after a month of usage. You can also decide if some code pathways (like a legacy data format from an old service) are no longer worth maintaining code for… and just “squish” them instead.
